A curated corpus is an inventory. The mixture turns it into a training distribution. When available data exceeds the token budget, sampling weights decide which domains the model practices, which sources repeat, and which capabilities compete for finite parameters and compute.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. convert stored corpus sizes into realized training probabilities and epochs;
2. explain temperature sampling, transfer, interference, and curriculum schedules;
3. compare manual mixtures with DoReMi-, DSIR-, and proxy-training approaches;
4. separate scaling-law planning from data-quality optimization; and
5. design a fixed-compute mixture experiment with a precommitted decision rule.

## From available tokens to sampled tokens

If source $i$ contains $n_i$ tokens, sampling in direct proportion to size gives the largest source most of the budget. Temperature sampling can flatten the distribution:

$$
p_i=\frac{n_i^{\alpha}}{\sum_j n_j^{\alpha}},\qquad 0<\alpha\leq1.
$$

At $\alpha=1$, probability follows corpus size. A lower $\alpha$ increases the relative weight of smaller sources. It does not create information: a small source may be repeated for many epochs, increasing memorization and overfitting risk.

For each proposed weight, compute both expected tokens and expected epochs. A mixture manifest records the intended probabilities and the realized distribution after shuffling, unavailable shards, packing, and filtering.

## Transfer and interference

A source can improve tasks outside its own domain through positive transfer. Code may support structured reasoning; high-quality long-form text may improve several language tasks. The same source can interfere with other capabilities when it consumes too much of the budget or pushes the model toward a narrow format.

There is therefore no single “quality” axis. Mixture evaluation is multi-objective: held-out loss and tasks are reported per domain and language, alongside an aggregate chosen before the experiment. A Pareto frontier is often more informative than one weighted average.

## Optimizing the mixture

A **manual mixture** encodes expert priors and is easy to inspect, but it may conceal untested assumptions. [DoReMi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429) [@xie2023doremi] uses a small proxy model and domain losses to learn weights that improve performance on a target domain mixture. [DSIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03169) [@xie2023dsir] resamples data to better match a target distribution. [DataComp-LM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794) [@li2024datacomplm] provides a controlled testbed for filtering and mixing strategies.

These methods do not eliminate judgment. The domain partition, target distribution, proxy size, metric suite, and transfer from proxy to final scale remain experimental assumptions.

## Curriculum and staged pretraining

A static mixture uses one probability distribution throughout training. A curriculum changes it with training step. A system may begin with broad natural language, increase code or mathematics later, or use a cooldown on a higher-quality distribution.

Ordering adds a causal variable. If the final checkpoint improves, the explanation may be the new data, its late position, the learning-rate phase, or their interaction. Compare a staged schedule with a static mixture containing the same total tokens.

## Scaling laws do not select the data

[Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) [@kaplan2020scaling] and [Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) [@hoffmann2022chinchilla] study relationships among model size, data quantity, compute, and loss under specified training distributions and assumptions.

These results help allocate a compute budget. They do not say which documents should fill the token budget. Two mixtures with equal token count and training FLOPs can produce different capability profiles. Data quality, coverage, transfer, interference, repetition, and tokenizer efficiency remain outside a simple token–parameter ratio.

## Studio: a three-mixture proxy experiment

Allocate a hypothetical three-billion-token budget across web, code, mathematics, scientific text, and multilingual sources. Construct:

1. a size-proportional baseline;
2. a manually justified balanced mixture; and
3. a proxy-selected or target-resampled mixture.

Train the same small model for the same tokens with the same optimizer schedule and seeds. Report realized weights, epochs, per-domain held-out loss, capability slices, uncertainty, and the Pareto frontier. Write the selection rule before viewing the final results.

## What to remember

1. The mixture—not the stored corpus—defines the pretraining distribution.
2. Up-sampling increases representation by repeating a finite source.
3. Transfer and interference make mixture selection multi-objective.
4. DoReMi, DSIR, and proxy training shift judgment into domains, targets, and proxy assumptions.
5. Curriculum must be compared with a static token-matched control.
6. Scaling laws allocate compute; they do not determine which data deserves it.
